items.secTitle: The Difference Quotient and Its Limit
items.caption: Secant through P₁ and P₂: m = Δy/Δx = 1.93
items.text: The two marked points are a and a + h on the curve; the rise Δy over the run Δx is the difference quotient, drawn as the slope of the secant line through them, 1.93 here. Slide P₂ toward P₁ and the secant turns into the tangent while its slope settles on the derivative. Drag the second point in on the

items.caption: Horizontal tangent: slope = 0.00 at a local maximum
items.text: At the marked point the tangent line is level and the slope readout is exactly zero: the function has stopped rising and is about to fall, which is what a critical point looks like on the graph. To the left the tangents tilt up, to the right they tilt down, the sign change the first derivative test reads. Slide the point across the hilltop on the
items.linkText: tangent line at a point tool

items.caption: f″(c) = 0.00 at an inflection point
items.text: The second derivative is read off the bend of the curve: positive where it cups upward, negative where it cups downward, and zero at the marked point where the bending switches sides. That switch is the inflection point, and f″ changes sign through it. Move the marker into either bend and watch f″(c) leave zero on the

items.caption: f(x) = x² and f′(x) = 2x, marked at x = 1
items.text: The upper curve is the function, the lower one its derivative, and at x = 1 the marker reads f′(1) = 2, the slope of the parabola there. The derivative is a straight line because bringing the exponent down leaves degree one: that is the power rule drawn out. Move the marker and watch the slope of the parabola track the height of the line on the

items.caption: f(x) = sin x and f′(x) = cos x, marked at x = 1
items.text: The derivative curve peaks where the sine climbs fastest, at x = 0, and crosses zero where the sine tops out, at π/2: the cosine is the sine’s slope read off point by point. At x = 1 the marker reads cos 1 ≈ 0.54. Slide the marker to a peak of the sine and watch the derivative hit zero on the

items.caption: f(x) = eˆx and f′(x) = eˆx coincide
items.text: The two curves lie exactly on top of each other: at every x the slope of eˆx equals its height, so at x = 1 both readings are e ≈ 2.72. No other function has this property, which is why e is the natural base. Check any point and see the two readouts agree on the

items.caption: f(x) = ln x and f′(x) = 1/x, marked at x = 1
items.text: The logarithm climbs steeply near zero and flattens as x grows, and its derivative curve 1/x records exactly that: large on the left, small on the right, equal to 1 at x = 1 where the marker sits. Move the marker toward zero and watch the slope reading run away on the

items.caption: Jump at x = 0: the two sides disagree
items.text: Approaching zero from the left the function heads to 0, from the right it sits at 1, and the checker’s three conditions fail at the second: no two-sided limit, so no continuity, so no derivative. A tangent line would have to be two different lines at once. Test any breakpoint against the three conditions on the

items.caption: The tangent line at P is the linear approximation
items.text: Near the marked point the curve and its tangent line are nearly indistinguishable, and the line’s slope, 1.89, is the f′(a) of the formula: moving dx along the line raises it by 1.89 dx, which is dy. The gap between line and curve, visible only farther out, is the error the differential ignores. Move the point and watch the approximating line follow on the
items.linkText: tangent line at a point tool

items.caption: f(x) = x³ above, f′(x) = 3x² below
items.text: Wherever the cubic rises its derivative sits above the axis, and at x = 0, where the cubic flattens for an instant, the derivative touches zero without crossing: the graph of f′ is read off the slopes of f. At the marker, x = 1, the cubic has slope 3 and the parabola has height 3. Slide the marker and watch height below follow slope above on the

items.page: Graph Analysis with Derivatives: Extrema & Curves
items.caption: Tangent at P with slope f′(c) = 1.89
items.text: The line touches the curve at P and nowhere else nearby, and its slope 1.89 is the derivative at that point; the point-slope equation of the section is this line written out. Where the curve is steeper the line tilts more, where the curve flattens the line goes level. Drag P along the curve and read the slope on the
items.linkText: tangent line at a point tool

items.page: Graph Analysis with Derivatives: Extrema & Curves
items.caption: x³ − 3x on [−3, 3]: critical points at x = ±1
items.text: The derivative 3x² − 3 vanishes at x = −1 and x = 1, and the tool marks both: a local maximum on the left, a local minimum on the right, each with a horizontal tangent. Nothing else in the interval is a candidate for an extreme except the two endpoints. Change the interval or the function and watch the candidates recomputed on the

items.page: Graph Analysis with Derivatives: Extrema & Curves
items.caption: f″(c) = 2.60: concave up, a cup
items.text: At the marked point the curve bends upward and the second derivative is positive; a horizontal tangent here would sit at the bottom of the cup, which is the local-minimum case of the second derivative test. Turn the bend over and the sign flips with it. Move the marker to a downward bend on the

items.page: Graph Analysis with Derivatives: Extrema & Curves
items.caption: f″(c) = −2.60: concave down
items.text: Here the slopes decrease as x increases: the tangent lines turn clockwise as they move right, and the curve stays below each of them. That is concavity read from the second derivative, negative throughout this stretch. Compare the two bends side by side on the

items.page: Graph Analysis with Derivatives: Extrema & Curves
items.caption: f″(c) = 0.00: the bending changes sides
items.text: To the left of the marker the curve cups down, to the right it cups up, and at the marker itself the second derivative is exactly zero while it changes sign: the definition of an inflection point in one picture. A zero of f″ without the sign change would not qualify. Slide the marker through the crossing on the

items.page: Graph Analysis with Derivatives: Extrema & Curves
items.caption: x⁴ − 4x² on [−3, 3]: critical points and endpoints
items.text: The W-shaped quartic has three critical points, two minima at x = ±√2 and a local maximum at 0, and the tool lists them beside the two endpoints; the absolute extremes on the closed interval are found by comparing just these five values. That is the Extreme Value Theorem turned into a procedure. Narrow the interval and watch the absolute maximum move to an endpoint on the

items.page: Higher Order Derivatives: Second, Third & nth
items.caption: f″(c) = 2.60: the slope is increasing
items.text: The first derivative says whether the curve rises; the second says whether the rise is speeding up. At the marker the tangent slopes are growing as x increases, the curve bends upward, and the readout f″(c) = 2.60 records how fast. Where the readout turns negative the bend has flipped. Watch the number and the bend change together on the

items.caption: Secant over [a, b] and the parallel tangent at c
items.text: The dashed line joins the endpoints of the interval and has slope (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a); the solid tangent at the marked c has the same slope, so the two lines are parallel. The theorem promises such a c on any interval where the function is smooth, and for the parabola there is exactly one. Change the interval and watch c move to keep the tangent parallel on the

items.caption: Identity, frozen at x0 = 1
items.text: f is the 45-degree line, f′ the flat dashed line at height 1. The tangent lies exactly on f, because a straight line is its own tangent everywhere.

items.secTitle: Quadratic: a Derivative That Grows Linearly
items.caption: Quadratic, frozen at x0 = 1
items.text: The parabola with its derivative drawn as the line f′(x) = 2x. At x0 = 1 the tangent slope is 2 and the dashed line passes through height 2 - the same number in two places.

items.secTitle: Cubic: a Flat Spot That Is Not an Extremum
items.caption: Cubic, frozen at x0 = 1
items.text: f′(x) = 3x² sits entirely above the axis apart from a single touch at the origin. That touch without a crossing is why x³ has a flat spot but no turning point.

items.secTitle: Sine: the Derivative Is a Quarter Turn
items.caption: Sine, frozen at x0 = 1
items.text: Two waves a quarter period apart. The marker on f′ reads 0.54 while f reads 0.84 - the sine is still rising, but slowing as it approaches its peak.

items.secTitle: Cosine: the Same Wave With a Sign
items.caption: Cosine, frozen at x0 = 1
items.text: The same pair with the roles swapped and a sign attached: f reads 0.54 and f′ reads -0.84. The dashed curve is below the axis wherever the cosine is falling.

items.caption: Exponential, frozen at x0 = 1
items.text: Solid and dashed curves coincide across the whole frame, and both markers land at 2.72. This is the graph of a function equal to its own derivative.

items.secTitle: Logarithm: a Derivative That Blows Up
items.caption: Logarithm, frozen at x0 = 1
items.text: Nothing is drawn left of the y-axis: both ln x and 1/x are undefined there. At x0 = 1 the log crosses zero while its derivative reads exactly 1.

items.secTitle: Identity: Every Point Is a c
items.caption: Identity on [-2, 2], frozen
items.text: Secant, curve and tangents all coincide, because f′ is 1 everywhere and the secant slope is also 1. The solver returns hundreds of valid c values here; the frozen picture keeps four of them, which looks identical since every tangent is the same line.

items.caption: Quadratic on [-2, 2], frozen
items.text: Equal endpoint heights make the secant horizontal, so the single tangent at c = 0 is horizontal too. This is the Rolle configuration.

items.caption: Cubic on [-2, 2], frozen
items.text: Three parallel lines at slope 4: the secant, plus tangents at c = -1.1547 and c = +1.1547. Two solutions, both drawn.

items.secTitle: Sine: a Full Period With a Flat Secant
items.caption: Sine on [0, 2π], frozen
items.text: A full period returns to its starting height, so the secant is flat and the two tangents sit at the crest and the trough - c = π/2 and c = 3π/2.

items.secTitle: Cosine: a Secant That Is Not Flat
items.caption: Cosine on [0, π], frozen
items.text: The first family with a genuinely tilted secant, at slope -0.6366. The two tangents are parallel to it, placed symmetrically about the midpoint.

items.secTitle: Exponential: Where the Average Rate Is Attained
items.caption: Exponential on [0, 1], frozen
items.text: One tangent, at c = 0.5413, matching the secant slope e - 1 = 1.7183. Note it sits right of the interval midpoint rather than on it.

items.secTitle: Quadratic: One Critical Point, No Ambiguity
items.caption: Quadratic on [-3, 3], frozen
items.text: One marker, at the origin. f′ is the line 2x crossing zero there, and f″ is the constant 2 lying flat above the axis - concave up everywhere, so the minimum is global.

items.secTitle: x³ − 3x: a Maximum and a Minimum
items.caption: x³ - 3x on [-3, 3], frozen
items.text: Two markers in different colours: a local max at x = -1 where f″ = -6, and a local min at x = +1 where f″ = +6. The dotted f″ line crosses zero between them, at the inflection.

items.secTitle: x³: Where the Second-Derivative Test Fails
items.caption: x³ on [-3, 3], frozen
items.text: A single grey-blue marker at the origin, labelled inflection (touch). f′ = 3x² sits on the axis there without crossing it, which is exactly the case the second-derivative test cannot decide.

items.secTitle: x⁴ − 4x²: Three Critical Points in a W
items.caption: x⁴ - 4x² on [-3, 3], frozen
items.text: Three markers: minima at ±1.4142 tied at f = -4, and a local max at the origin sitting at f = 0 - above both minima, and still only a local maximum.

items.secTitle: sin(x): Four Critical Points Over Two Periods
items.caption: sin(x) on [-2π, 2π], frozen
items.text: Four markers alternating max, min, max, min at ±π/2 and ±3π/2. Widen the window and the tool just finds more of the same two heights.

items.secTitle: The Gaussian: One Maximum and Two Inflections That Are Not Critical
items.caption: e^(-x²) on [-3, 3], frozen
items.text: One marker at the peak. The dotted f″ curve crosses zero at ±0.707 - the two inflection points on the shoulders - but neither is marked, because f′ is not zero there.

items.caption: f(t) = t³ shaded from 0 to 2; F(2) = 4
items.text: The shaded region under the curve from 0 to x = 2 is the definite integral, a number, 4; letting the right edge x move produces the accumulation function F(x) = x⁴/4, an antiderivative of f. One picture holds both meanings of the integral sign: area for fixed limits, function for a moving one. Drag the right edge and watch F grow on the

items.caption: Midpoint sum for x² on [0, 3] with n = 8
items.text: Eight rectangles of width 3/8 stand on the interval, each as tall as the curve at the middle of its strip; their total area approximates the area under the parabola, 9. Doubling n halves the width and the error shrinks with it, and the limit of that process is the definite integral. Raise n and watch the sum close in on the

items.caption: Left-endpoint sum for x² on [0, 3], n = 8
items.text: The interval is cut into eight strips of width Δx = 3/8 and each rectangle takes the height of the curve at the left end of its strip; because the parabola rises, every rectangle falls short and the sum underestimates the area, 9. Choose the right endpoints instead and every rectangle overshoots. Switch the sample point and increase n on the

items.caption: sin t from 0 to 2: area counted with sign
items.text: The shading follows the curve above the axis, and if the right edge were pushed past π the shading below the axis would count as negative: the accumulated value rises while the curve is above the axis and falls while it is below. Here, from 0 to 2, the total is 1 − cos 2 ≈ 1.42. Push the right edge past π and watch the total start to shrink on the

items.caption: ∫₀² t² dt = F(2) − F(0) = 8/3
items.text: The shaded area is the definite integral, and the accumulation curve above it reads F(2) = 8/3 exactly: the antiderivative t³/3 evaluated at the right edge minus its value at the left. No rectangles were summed to get the number. Move the right edge and read the area straight off the antiderivative on the

items.caption: 1/x² near x = 0: the integrand is unbounded
items.text: Both probes, at −0.5 and 0.5, read 4, and moving them inward sends the values to infinity: the curve has a vertical asymptote at 0, so no rectangle of finite height can cover the region beside it. An integral across this point must stop short at t and let t approach 0 in a limit. Squeeze the probes toward the asymptote on the

items.caption: F(x) = ∫₀ˆx t² dt = x³/3 is an antiderivative of x²
items.text: The lower curve is f(t) = t² and the upper one is the area accumulated under it from 0; the slope of the upper curve at any x equals the height of the lower one there, which is what F′ = f means. Start the accumulation from a different a and the upper curve shifts by a constant: the + C of the indefinite integral. Change the starting point and watch the whole antiderivative slide on the

items.caption: F(x) = ∫₀ˆx t³ dt with x = 2: F′(2) = f(2) = 8
items.text: The accumulation function is the upper curve; at the right edge x = 2 its slope equals the height of the integrand there, 8. Nudging x to the right adds a thin strip of area whose height is f(x) and whose width is the nudge, so the rate at which area accumulates is f(x) itself. Move the edge and compare the slope above with the height below on the

items.secTitle: Left Rule: Every Rectangle Falls Short
items.caption: Left rule, frozen at n = 8
items.text: Every rectangle top meets the curve at its left edge and falls away below it after that. The eight gaps between the tops and the curve are the -1.6172 of error, drawn to scale.

items.caption: Right rule, frozen at n = 8
items.text: The mirror image: each top meets the curve at its right edge, so the whole strip sits above the curve. The overshoot of +1.7578 is the visible excess.

items.secTitle: Midpoint Rule: Errors That Cancel Inside Each Strip
items.caption: Midpoint rule, frozen at n = 8
items.text: Each rectangle now crosses the curve rather than clearing it, too high on one side of the strip and too low on the other. What is left over after they cancel is -0.0352.

items.secTitle: Trapezoid Rule: Joining the Sample Points
items.caption: Trapezoid rule, frozen at n = 8
items.text: The only method whose outline slants with the curve: each cap is the chord between the two strip edges. On an upward-curving function the chord rides above, giving +0.0703.

items.secTitle: Identity: Area That Grows Like a Triangle
items.caption: Identity, frozen at a = 0, x = 2
items.text: The shaded region is a triangle of area 2, and the dashed accumulator passes through height 2 at x = 2. A straight integrand gives a parabolic F.

items.caption: Quadratic, frozen at a = 0, x = 2
items.text: Two markers at different heights on the same vertical: f(2) = 4 is a height, F(2) = 2.667 is an accumulated area. The slope of the dashed curve there is 4, not 2.667.

items.secTitle: Cubic: a Faster Integrand, a Faster Accumulator
items.caption: Cubic, frozen at a = 0, x = 2
items.text: f(2) = 8 with an accumulated area of 4. F(x) = x⁴/4 climbs sharply past x = 1, and stays positive on the left of the axis even though the integrand is negative there.

items.secTitle: Sine: an Accumulator That Turns Around
items.caption: Sine, frozen at a = 0, x = 2
items.text: Area 1.416 collected so far, with the integrand at 0.909 and falling. Past x = π the shaded slivers go negative and the dashed accumulator turns back down.

items.secTitle: Cosine: Where the Two Curves Swap Roles
items.caption: Cosine, frozen at a = 0, x = 2
items.text: The integrand has already gone negative at -0.416 while the running total is still +0.909. The accumulator here is exactly sin(x) - the two curves are the familiar pair, swapped.

items.secTitle: Exponential: Accumulator and Integrand Almost Coincide
items.caption: Exponential, frozen at a = 0, x = 2
items.text: f(2) = 7.389 against F(2) = 6.389 - a gap of exactly 1, and the same gap at every x, because F(x) = eˣ - 1 is the integrand shifted down one unit.

items.secTitle: The Central Idea of a Limit
items.caption: (x² − 1)/(x − 1) near x = 1: the hole
items.text: The function has no value at 1, but the probes on either side, at 0.5 and 1.5, read 1.5 and 2.5, and closing in they both head for 2. That number is the limit, and it exists although f(1) does not: behaviour near the point, not at it. Slide the probes toward the hole on the

items.caption: √x at x = 0: only the right-hand approach exists
items.text: To the right of 0 the probe reads a value heading to 0; to the left there is no function at all, so the left-hand limit cannot even be asked. The right-hand limit is 0, and it is the only one available at an endpoint of the domain. Try to place the left probe on the

items.caption: 1/x² near x = 0: both sides run to +∞
items.text: The probes at −0.5 and 0.5 both read 4, and every step inward multiplies the readings: the outputs grow without bound while the inputs approach 0. That is an infinite limit, written lim = ∞, and the line x = 0 is a vertical asymptote. Watch the readings climb as the probes close in on the

items.caption: Wrong value at x = 1: the limit exists, f(1) misses it
items.text: Both approaches agree on a limit at x = 1, and f(1) is defined, yet the marked value sits away from where the curve is heading: the third condition fails and the function is not continuous there. Fixing the single value would repair it. See which of the three conditions each example fails on the

items.caption: Condition 3 fails: lim f(x) ≠ f(1)
items.text: The checker tests the three conditions in order: here f(1) is defined and the two-sided limit exists, but the marked point sits away from the limit, so the equality in condition 3 fails and the verdict is discontinuous. One relocated point would make the function continuous. Run the three-step check on any example on the

items.caption: Hole at x = 1: removable
items.text: The limit at 1 exists and equals 2, but the function has no value there; filling the single missing point would make the curve continuous, which is why the discontinuity is called removable. The simplified formula x + 1 is exactly that repaired function. Compare the hole with the repaired curve on the

items.caption: Jump at x = 0: left limit 0, right limit 1
items.text: From the left the function approaches 0, from the right it approaches 1, and no single value could bridge the gap: the two-sided limit does not exist, so condition 2 fails. The size of the jump is the difference of the two one-sided limits. Read the two one-sided values on the

items.caption: Asymptote at x = 0: the limit is infinite
items.text: Approaching 0 the function runs off the top or bottom of the picture: at least one one-sided limit is infinite, so there is no finite limit and no value that could be assigned. The vertical line x = 0 is the asymptote the curve hugs. Watch the readings blow up on the

items.caption: sin(1/x) near 0: no limit at all
items.text: The probes at ±0.5 read sin 2 ≈ 0.91, but moving them inward the readings swing between −1 and 1 faster and faster, never settling: the limit fails to exist not by running away but by refusing to choose. No value of f(0) could make this continuous. Squeeze the probes and watch the readings swing on the

items.caption: Step at x = 0: left limit 0, right limit 1
items.text: Evaluated from the left the probe heads to 0, from the right to 1; the two one-sided limits are perfectly well defined and simply differ, so the two-sided limit does not exist. Any expression that changes formula at a point, like |x|/x, has to be evaluated this way. Read each side separately on the

items.page: Limits and Infinity: Asymptotes & End Behavior
items.caption: 1/x²: a vertical asymptote at x = 0
items.text: Both probes read 4 at ±0.5 and grow without bound as they move in: both one-sided limits are +∞, which is the condition for a vertical asymptote at x = 0. The curve approaches the line without ever reaching it. Move the probes inward and watch the readings climb on the

items.page: Limits and Infinity: Asymptotes & End Behavior
items.caption: 1/x near 0: −∞ from the left, +∞ from the right
items.text: The left probe reads −2 and the right one 2, and moving inward they diverge in opposite directions: the two one-sided infinite limits have opposite signs, so the curve leaves the picture downward on one side of the asymptote and upward on the other. The two-sided limit does not exist even as an infinite limit. Compare the two signs on the

items.caption: √x at 0: a right-hand limit with no left-hand partner
items.text: Only the right probe can be placed, and it heads to 0; with no function to the left there is no left-hand limit to compare it with, so the two-sided limit is not defined at this endpoint although the one-sided one is. The equivalence in this section needs both sides to exist and agree. Try both probes on the

items.caption: The floor function: a jump at every integer
items.text: At each integer the function steps up by one: the left-hand limit is the lower step and the right-hand limit the upper one, so the two never agree and every integer is a jump discontinuity. Between integers the function is constant and perfectly continuous. Test the checker at an integer and at a non-integer on the

items.caption: 1/x at 0: −∞ on the left, +∞ on the right
items.text: The probes at ±0.5 read −2 and 2 and run off in opposite directions as they close in, which is exactly the sign pattern the section derives for 1/(x − 2) at 2: the side decides the sign. Watch the two readings separate on the

items.caption: x² at x = 1: both probes converge on 1
items.text: The left probe at 0.5 reads 0.25 and the right one at 1.5 reads 2.25, and as both move toward 1 the readings meet at 1: the two traces of the section converge to the same height, so the two-sided limit exists and equals f(1). Drag the probes in from both sides on the

items.secTitle: When Two-Sided Limits Fail to Exist
items.caption: Step at x = 0: the two traces end at different heights
items.text: Traced from the left the function heads to 0, from the right to 1: two well-defined one-sided limits that disagree, so the two-sided limit does not exist. This is the jump case of the section; the infinite and oscillating cases fail for different reasons. Watch the two probes refuse to meet on the

items.page: Tangent Line Visualizer at a Point
items.caption: Free drag, frozen at c = -0.5
items.text: No scenario is running - this is the widget at its default point of tangency. P sits at (-0.5, 0.46) and the slope readout gives f′(-0.5) = -0.75, so the tangent already leans downhill. Drag c anywhere and this same picture redraws with a new slope.

items.page: Tangent Line Visualizer at a Point
items.caption: Positive slope, frozen at c = -1.7
items.text: The tangent through P = (-1.7, 0.06) carries slope 1.89. Curve and line both climb to the right, and inside the shaded band every other tangent would climb as well.

items.page: Tangent Line Visualizer at a Point
items.caption: Negative slope, frozen at c = 0.4
items.text: The tangent through P = (0.4, -0.38) carries slope -0.84. The band spans (-1, 1), the whole interval on which the cubic descends from its peak to its valley.

items.page: Tangent Line Visualizer at a Point
items.secTitle: Horizontal Tangent at the Local Maximum
items.caption: Local maximum, frozen at c = -1
items.text: Slope 0: the tangent is a horizontal line through P = (-1, 0.67), the peak of the curve. The chevrons point uphill on the left and downhill on the right - the sign change that confirms a maximum.

items.page: Tangent Line Visualizer at a Point
items.secTitle: Horizontal Tangent at the Local Minimum
items.caption: Local minimum, frozen at c = 1
items.text: Slope 0 again, this time through P = (1, -0.67) at the bottom of the valley. The chevrons run downhill then uphill - the reversed sign change that confirms a minimum.

items.caption: Free drag, frozen at c = -0.5
items.text: No scenario running - the widget at its default point. f″(-0.5) = -1, so the badge reads negative and the tangent already sits above the curve. Drag c across zero and the gap flips colour.

items.secTitle: Concave Up: the Slope Is Increasing
items.caption: Concave up, frozen at c = 1.3
items.text: f″(1.3) = 2.6 > 0. The tangent through P runs below the curve, and the blue gap widens in both directions as the curve pulls away above the line.

items.secTitle: Concave Down: the Slope Is Decreasing
items.caption: Concave down, frozen at c = -1.3
items.text: f″(-1.3) = -2.6 < 0. The mirror image: the tangent lies above the curve and the red gap opens downward. The local maximum at x = -1 sits inside this same region.

items.caption: Inflection, frozen at c = 0
items.text: f″(0) = 0 and the sign flips across c. The tangent crosses the curve rather than staying on one side, and the gap is red to the left of c, blue to the right - the concavity change made visible.

items.secTitle: Direct Hit: Four Steps from x₀ = 3
items.caption: Direct hit, frozen after 4 iterations
items.text: Four tangents, each steep enough to keep its correction small. The P-markers crowd together as they approach α, and the final iterate x3 = 2.095136 is already correct to three decimals.

items.secTitle: Crosses Over: One Tangent Throws the Guess Across the Root
items.caption: Crosses over, frozen after 5 iterations
items.text: The leftmost tangent, at x0 = -1, is the shallow one: it carries the guess clear across the root to x1 = 3. The remaining four steps repeat the direct-hit run exactly.

items.secTitle: Stalls: What Happens Near a Critical Point
items.caption: Stalls, frozen at the failing step
items.text: f′(0.85) = 0.1675 makes the tangent nearly horizontal, so it meets the axis at x1 = 37.18 - far off the right edge, which is what the red arrow marks. The frame is the step itself, before the tool clears it.

items.secTitle: Stepping Manually from a Custom Start
items.caption: Manual start, frozen at x0 = 3
items.text: Nothing has run yet: just the draggable x0 on the axis, the drop line up to P0 on the curve, and the grey marker at the root α ≈ 2.0946. Every Step click adds one tangent to this picture.

items.caption: Ascending, frozen at the end of the run
items.text: Both points on the rising left wing, Δx = 0.70 and Δy = 1.35, so the secant slope is +1.93. Every chevron in the shaded band points the same way the secant does.

items.caption: Descending, frozen at the end of the run
items.text: A symmetric interval about the origin: Δy = -0.99 over Δx = 1.10 gives -0.90. The band covers (-1, 1), where the derivative is negative at every single point.

items.secTitle: Closing In on the Local Maximum
items.caption: Local max, frozen after both tighten steps
items.text: The final pair, [-1.08, -0.92]. The points have closed to within 0.16 of each other and the secant has flattened to m = 0.00 - the limit being f′(-1) = 0.

items.secTitle: Closing In on the Local Minimum
items.caption: Local min, frozen after both tighten steps
items.text: The mirror image at [0.92, 1.08], with the same flattened secant. The chevrons reverse: down on the approach, up on the way out.

items.caption: Free drag, frozen at the default pair
items.text: No scenario running: P1 at x = -1.40 and P2 at x = -0.40, the positions Reset returns to. The secant reads m = -0.11 - very slightly falling, because the interval straddles the peak unevenly.

items.caption: Smooth, frozen at c = 0
items.text: f(x) = x² with the probe at the origin. One L line, one marker, nothing else to see - f(c), L⁻ and L⁺ all read 0 and the three checks pass.

items.caption: Hole, frozen at c = 1
items.text: The L line sits at 2 and the curve passes straight through that level, but no f(c) marker sits on it: the function has no value at x = 1. Condition 1 is the one that fails.

items.caption: Jump, frozen at c = 0
items.text: Two L lines instead of one, at 0 and at 1. The closed endpoint belongs to the upper piece and the open one to the lower - the visual signature of one-sided limits that disagree.

items.secTitle: Wrong Value: the Limit Exists but Misses
items.caption: Wrong value, frozen at c = 1
items.text: The L line is at 2 where the line would go, while the f(c) marker sits alone at 0. Both are drawn, and the vertical distance between them is the failure of condition 3.

items.caption: Asymptote, frozen at c = 0
items.text: f(x) = 1/x² climbing off the top of the frame on both sides. No L lines are drawn at all, because neither one-sided limit is finite.

items.caption: Staircase, frozen at c = -2
items.text: Each step carries a closed endpoint on the left and an open one on the right. L⁻ = -2.5 and L⁺ = -1.5 straddle the step, and the same picture repeats at every integer.

items.caption: Quadratic, frozen at c = 1, ε = 0.5
items.text: One L line at height 1, with the f(c) marker sitting on it and the two approach markers straddling c at 0.25 and 2.25. Everything agrees - this is the case with nothing to diagnose.

items.secTitle: Hole: the Limit Exists Without the Value
items.caption: Hole, frozen at c = 1, ε = 0.5
items.text: The L line is drawn at 2 and the approach markers close in on it from 1.5 and 2.5, but the line carries no f(c) marker: the value at c is missing while the limit is not.

items.caption: Step, frozen at c = 0, ε = 0.5
items.text: Two L lines, at 0 and at 1, with an open endpoint below and a closed one above. The approach markers at -0.5 and 1.5 are heading for different heights.

items.secTitle: 1/x²: Both Sides Blow Up the Same Way
items.caption: 1/x², frozen at c = 0, ε = 0.5
items.text: No L lines at all - there is no finite height to draw one at. Both approach markers read 4 and climb together as ε shrinks.

items.caption: 1/x, frozen at c = 0, ε = 0.5
items.text: The same missing L lines, but the two branches leave the frame in opposite directions. The approach markers read -2 and +2 and separate further with every reduction of ε.

items.secTitle: sin(1/x): Oscillation With No Limit at All
items.caption: sin(1/x), frozen at c = 0, ε = 0.5
items.text: The curve stays inside [-1, 1] yet packs more and more oscillations toward c. The two approach markers read -0.91 and 0.91 here, and would read something quite different at any other ε.

items.secTitle: Square Root: a Limit From One Side Only
items.caption: Square root, frozen at c = 0, ε = 0.5
items.text: Nothing is drawn left of c, so only one approach marker exists, at 0.71. The closed endpoint at the origin is where the right-hand limit lands.
